My information is that
the contract for this work was let to a gentleman by the name of Boone, whom I know very well. I understand that the work involved very considerable difficulty and that the department took over the work. I should like full information on this item. Mr. Boone is a very competent contractor. He has done a very great deal of work in the province of New Brunswick; he happens to be one of my constituents, and I know him very well. I am wondering just what the trouble was and how the government proposes to use him. Some of the workmen, I might point out, have not been paid. One of them came to see me just before I left home, and told me that the government engineer at Halifax, who was then in charge of the work, which I understand has been suspended1 on account of the season, had assured them that they would all be paid. I know that some of these men have not been paid, and I think that the government ought to see that they are paid. That is only one phase of the situation.
I think we ought to have a very full explanation from the minister as to the position of this contract.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The contract was let on September 22, 1928, to Mr. Boone, an order in council f\Tr. Mackenzie King.]
having been passed accepting his tender for the construction of pier No. 5. The work did not proceed in accordance with the contract, and it was taken out of Mr. Boone's hands and proceeded with by the district engineer. As far as the sub-contractors are concerned, when a contract gets into that position, it takes a little time to make all the necessary adjustments, but I understand that these matters are being looked after.

The minister has not quite covered the ground. I have no brief for Mr Boone. He has not retained me or consulted me, but I have been consulted by some of the men who have not received their pay for the work they did previous to the government taking over the contract. I am very much surprised to hear that Mr. Boone has fallen down on this job, and I would like to know what the trouble is. The minister said that he did not proceed in accordance with the contract. Mr. Boone is a very capable man. He has plant, machinery and equipment; he has experience and he has capital. How was Mr. Boone used? Was he simply shouldered off the job? I would like the details. I do not question the minister's word as to anything he said, but he has not said anything, and that is the fault I have to find. For a lawyer I am rather surprised that he is so sparing of information. If there is anything damaging to Mr. Boone in connection with the contract, let us have it, because I am satisfied that he will have an answer.

I can give the whole particulars if my hon. friend wishes them, but I have not them at hand. My information is that Mr. Boone took the contract, started upon the work, quit it, was notified to proceed at various times and did not proceed, and it was not until he had been notified and bad omitted to proceed with the contract that steps were taken to have the work carried on under the direction of the engineer.

That being the case, will
the minister produce some evidence to support that statement?
Yes.

I would like to know what you. are going to do about the unpaid workmen? Are they to be allowed to starve? The men worked up to the time the contract was taken over by the government. I am not saying that it was taken over wrongly or improperly; I do not know; I am looking for

information. But I do know that one man at least needs the money that is owing to him. He has waited all winter for it. I told him that he had better get after Mr. Boone, who is quite capable of paying these men.
Quite so. You are right.

But the government must
have this man's deposit in their hands.

Yes, he must have put
up a deposit. It is the government's business to look after the employees.

No.

I think the minister had
better let the item stand until we get more information.

I shall be very glad to
furnish my hon. friend with all the information.

I am not making any
charges against the department. I am looking for information. The minister's statement so far as it has gone is all right, but let us have the whole facts.

I can probably get all
the information before six o'clock, and I am quite sure that I can satisfy my hon. friend that the matter has been proceeded with in the usual way. What my hon. friend has said with regard to Mr. Boone I understand to be true, that he is a man of substance and quite capable of paying all these people to whom he owes any obligation.

In that connection may I
say that the gentleman who interviewed me told me that the engineer said that the government would pay him and the other workmen, but that promise, if made, has not been implemented. I do not say that it was made, but I believe the man was truthful, and certainly the government have it in their power to pay these men from one source or another, out of the progress estimates, out of the drawback or out of the deposit.

is this wharf?

North-Victoria.

whereabouts?

west of Baie St. Lawrence near the northern extremity of Cape Breton Island.

Where is this?

I can tell my hon.
friend where it is. It is a very important fishing centre in my county, and I am very glad to see an item in the estimates for this very much needed work. How is this work to be done-by contract or by day labour? If by contract, who is the contractor?
It will be done by contract; that is the expectation.

Will the fair-wage
clause be introduced and enforced on this work?

That clause is in all the
contracts made by the Public Works department.

But it is enforced
in very few of them. On all the public works in my county the men are working ten hours a day at 25 cents an hour-$250 a day. I feel that that is unfair and does not fulfil the requirements of the fair-wage clause. I think something should be done about it, not only in my own county but in every place throughout the Dominion where public works are being carried on.

This is the first intimation I have had of anything in the nature of a complaint. Nothing has reached me that unfair wages are being paid. All our contracts contain the fair-wage clause; that is, wages satisfactory to the Department of Labour are being paid on these contracts.

Last session a certain amount of money was voted for works on the harbour in the town of Inverness, and the wages there paid on the average were only twenty-five cents per hour for a ten-hour day. I do not think that is giving the labourers of this country a fair deal. Last session when I criticised the Department of Labour the hon. minister (Mr. Heenan) promised me definitely that a bill would be introduced this session to enforce the fair-wage clause. It has not been introduced. It seems to me that the government should set an example to private corporations in the matter of wages. Does the Minister of Labour intend to introduce that bill this session, in accordance with his promise last year?

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, N.S.

Mr. Chairman, you will
understand that my estimates are not under consideration just now.
Don't be so nervous.

This is the first time I
have ever been accused of nervousness. If the prevailing rates of wages are not being paid in my hon. friend's district, one reason is that we have received no complaints that such is the case. We have a fair-wage officer for the maritime provinces who goes around checking up wages.
And making votes.
And enforcing the fairwage clause where there are any complaints.

All I have to say is, if
the statement of the minister is correct, officers of other departments of the government are complaining to the foremen in charge of public works that the wages being paid are too high, although the wages are much lower than those required by the fair-wage clause under similar circumstances.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that our officer is raising the wages on public works above that which prevails in the district ?

No. I did not say anything of the kind. I said if the minister's statement was correct, other officers of the government -not in his department-are complaining to the foremen in charge of construction work that the wages paid are too high, while those wages are below the wages called for by the fair-wage clause.

Is the fair-wage clause
posted up so that all men can see it?
Yes.
Yes.
Absolutely not.
Is the notice posted up where every man can see it?
Those are the instructions given by the department.

I may say for the information of the minister that during the past year various public works have been constructed in my constituency, and no fair-wage clause has been posted up; in fact everything has been done as secretly as possible. Furthermore, the general public are not permitted to get an opportunity to ask for work. They must come and promise under oath that they will support the party, and then they get $2.50 a day.

Hear, hear. In Halifax in
particular.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should dismiss this matter too lightly, for it is very important. If organized or unorganized labour in this country is to be given a chance at all, the first body to set a good example in the matter of wages should be the government of Canada. I am particularly pressing this point because of the definite promise made by the Minister of Labour last session, in response to criticisms levelled against government contracts by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. WToodsworth) and myself, that something would be done this session to see that the fair-wage clause not only would be inserted in all government contracts but that fair wages would be paid in all such cases. Now, fair wages are not being paid on all government contracts. In my own town of Inverness last year certain people withdrew their young men from public works because the wages were too low. These young men, about twenty years of age, were working on one of these government works, employment of a very trying nature, for 25 cents an hour, working ten hours a day. As a matter of fact in that community the minimum wage is $3.25. Not to apply this rate on public works is an absolutely unfair condition of things. I want to see public works constructed, but at the same time I want to see the men who work on them given a chance to live.

Does the Minister of Public
Works admit that the men employed there were receiving only 25 cents an hour?

I cannot tell what amount the contractor is paying his men in each case unless a complaint is made, when we have it investigated, or unless the engineer or whoever is in charge goes around to the work and finds that less than the regular wages are being paid. Our experience has been that fair wages are usually paid, or else there is a complaint. In the cases in question, we have had no complaint.

Supposing it is a fact that
these men have been receiving only 25 cents an hour, when they were supposed to be receiving 334 cents per hour under the fair-wage clause, will the Department of Labour see to it that these men get back the difference in pay?

Just let me say this: If any hon. member of this house can show me where the men have not been receiving the prevailing rate of wages I will undertake to

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, N.S.
collect the difference between what they have been paid and what they should have been paid. This last year we have collected thousands of dollars in back pay, where we have been able to find such cases.

Is it not specifically mentioned in each contract what the prevailing rate of wages in that part of the country shall be. It is always specified in any big contracts that are let what the prevailing rate of wages shall be for labour.

I was not referring to work carried on by contract. I was referring to work carried on by the government itself through foremen appointed by them, recommended by a certain man who had 'the patronage in the county. The engineer comes along and tells the foreman that he is paying too much. That is the situation.
Mr. ARTHUR'S: Will the Minister of Labour state whether he has had any complaints from 'that particular province.
Yes, we have investigated-
How many complaints has this officer reported, so far as government works are concerned, in the province of Nova Scotia?
We generally get the complaint from the men, and then an officer goes to adjust it. We do not get the complaint from the officer himself.
I thought the minister said a few moments ago that he had an officer in Nova Scotia whose duty it was to visit the various public works to see that the men received proper pay.
May I ask the Minister of Labour if he knows of the labour unions being consulted as to what the standard rates of wages are.
We consult everybody.

The minister cannot get away with any statement like that. There is a great deal of money being spent in my constituency by day labour, and I will tell you the little man who is consulted. His name is Peter J. Hughes. He was the man who stuck himself up the night before nomination day to run against me. He is a decent mao. I have not anything against Peter Hughes, but he is the man who is consulted, and the minister cannot get away with any statement like that, so far as I am concerned, because I know that what I say is tme. And I know who the foreman is and the foreman tells me that he was only to hire such men as
Hughes told him to hire, and he was only [DOT]to pay such wages as were agreed upon in the same area. The minister cannot say that he consults everybody, because we know to the contrary.
And I want, to say to you that an bon. member cannot get away with that with the Minister of Labour either.
Don't sidestep.
I am not afraid of the hon. minister.

If there is any department of the government that is out of politics it is the Labour department. There is neither a member of parliament nor a defeated candidate consulted in the matter of labour disputes or fair wages.

Nobody is talking about
that.

The Minister of Labour says that the Labour department is out of politics. Well, if there is any department of this government that is absolutely in politics it is the Labour department. The Minister of Labour deserted his duties as the Minister of Labour in the federal parliament during the last provincial election and toured all over the north country, going into practically every constituency, riding in airplanes, probably at the expense of this country, at the same time boasting what they were going to do to Howard Ferguson in that election.

And incidentally made bets from the platform.
Mr. HEENAiN: I thought my hon. friend invited me to go to Fort William.
Yes, and if he does as much harm to his party in my election as he did in the provincial election I hope he comes and stays there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He did not take his department along with him.

We are having a rather interesting discussion. This is a matter that should 'be aired on the floor of the house some time, and we might as well do it now. In respect to the contention of the hon. minister that no politics have been played in the matter of fair wages, and that the labour unions are being consulted, I am not going to say that that is untrue, but I do say that in so far as my constituency is concerned it is absolutely not the fact, and if he has heard anything to the contrary it is absolutely wrong. The man who is consulted is the defeated

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, N.S.
Liberal candidate, and before you can get a job on a public work commanding the magnificent sum of 25 cents an hour for ten hours a day you have to have a written form signed by that defeated candidate, and I know that to be true. I am not protesting against that on political grounds because it is the beet thing that could possibly happen to me politically. In the town of Inverness some Liberals left that work because they were not being paid a living wage. I do not wish to introduce any politics into this. We are all very sincere when we make that statement. But what I am interested in is this: I take the stand that on public works in this country a living wage should be paid to the people who are working there no matter how they got there, so long as they are doing an honest day's work. The hon. Minister of Labour last year-and I want to emphatically recall this to his mind-definitely promised that some action would be taken this year; he promised my friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and myself when his estimates were under discussion last year that legislation would be introduced providing for a living wage for men who work on government works. Now, that has not been done and I am very much interested in that. I believe every hon. member no matter to what political party he belongs is also interested, and I want to ask the minister if he intends to do that this session, and if not, why not? I think I am entitled to a reply from my hon. friend. This is a serious matter, and when he makes a serious promise he cannot throw it lightly aside.
The Minister of Labour's estimates are not under consideration now.

It does not matter. Your action is under consideration now. It is not a matter of estimates at all. I am just asking, in this connection, whether you are introducing legislation at this session. If you are, I would like you to tell the house.

Mr. Chairman, we are 'told that there have 'been no complaints to reach either the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Labour that the fair wage has not been given to those workmen. This government of all governments is appointing officers throughout the country at large salaries to do the work. Let them appoint overseers or inspectors whose duty it will be to inspect every public work and see that the workmen get the fair wage. Why do they not do that instead of asking the poor man-as they were asking the poor soldier the other day, to prove his case-to make the complaint him-
self. The first thing a workman finds when be makes a complaint is that he has lost his j ob. If an inspector appointed by the government is on the job to see that the contractor pays the fair wage all that will be done away with.

I am rather astonished to find that the methods quoted by my friend to my right are entirely different from those found in my own experience. You will remember that last year this house voted a considerable sum of money to build the Calgary post office. One of the first things I found there was that the Minister of Labour had sent down a fair wage officer who consulted both unions there as to what the standard of wages should be. At that particular time I wrote to the Minister of Public Works suggesting to him that only people who were residents of Calgary should be engaged upon the work. I received a very abrupt reply from the Minister of Public Works, in which be said this was a Dominion concern and that they could not refuse employment to any Canadian citizen.
May I ask a question? Was there any defeated Liberal candidate there?

No, there was not; I do not know about the riding itself, but I suppose there was in West Calgary. However, as far as I was concerned there were no politics in the matter and I believe there was no discrimination shown as between the different unions. I know the president of one of the unions went down with me to see if the fair wage clause was posted up. It was not my business to look after that, but he found it and he said, "I am perfectly willing to confess that there are international union men engaged there, together with men of the allCanadian congress, and they are all receiving the same standard of wages." On the other hand, on the Ghost river construction last year men were being paid very low wages. We complained to the Minister of Labour about the matter and fought it with him for nearly a year, with the result that almost $20,000 in back wages was paid. Many a man received a Christmas present of $100 or more which he had not expected, and so I am rather astonished to find that while this was the case in one constituency it was not the case in another.

I have received through the mail from two or three friends of mine belonging to associations in the city of Toronto and throughout the province, copies of a draft bill with regard to fair wages which they had submitted to the minister, as I understand

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, N.S.
it, relying somewhat on an engagement of the government through the Minister of Labour last year to introduce such legislation during this session. I do not know very much about it, but I do remember the minister saying that he would undertake to submit legislation of that sort this year. Surely it is not unreasonable for the Minister of Labour, who is in his seat, to be expected to answer civil questions. This concerns his department, and the only construction 1 can put upon his refusal to answer is that he does not know anything about it. So man}- things in his department create a little suspicion, and there are so many things about which he does not know that I am not surprised at his inability to answer the question. Perhaps I might put it again: Are we to have such legislation this year.

All I can say just now is that in the Department of Labour we had a bill drafted, when the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada presented another bill of their own. That bill is now under consideration and I hope to be able to make a statement before very long as to what will be done in that connection.
That hardly deals with the case.
I have no intention of embarrassing the Minister of Labour at all-
Why not?
Oh, oh.

Because he is a warm personal friend of mine, but there is a little information I should like to get from him. He mentioned the fair wage officer down in Nova Scotia, implying that this man would see that justice was done. Perhaps he could give - us some information about the capabilities of that gentleman, as to whether he would know what was a fair wage. From what I know of him I do not think the man ever did a day's work in his life. That man has been down in my constituency; what he was doing there I do not know, but I have a shrewd suspicion that the gentleman was there on a political mission, in spite of the statement by the minister that there are no politics in his department.

I do not know the fair wage officer, or at least I did not know him until he entered the service; he was appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I might just say it is the prevailing rate of wages which we try to enforce on these contracts. It is
not a fair wage; that is a misnomer. It is the prevailing rate of wages in that district, and whether or not we will change that policy this session is for further consideration later on.

It is the one, no doubt, that this will be spent on.

I made some pretty strong remarks last year, in regard to the condition of one of those wharves, and the only thing I wonder at is that that wharf is still standing. I refer to the wharf with the railway freight shed on it. It is in an actually dangerous condition. Why not complete that wharf? Five thousand dollars is only putting a patch on a mitt. Why don't you finish it?

This is expected to do the work on the wharf that he says is in the worst condition. I think that is what they call the shed wharf, and it is not thought that any serious damage will result from letting the other work stand for another year. That is our report.
Am I to understand from the minister that the whole $5,000 will be spent on the shed wharf?
Yes.

And you will not complete the repairs to the low level wharf?
Mr. ELLIOTT. Not this year.
Why not?

Well, we are trying to do the things that are the most urgent, in the order of urgency. That is all I can say to 
my hon. friend. The fact that we are doing the one that is most in need this year is the best evidence he can have of the policy that we are following in these different repairs.
But the whole work is urgent and should have been done long ago. Why do you not complete it? What is the use of making two bites of a cherry?
Those are two cherries.
This is one of the jobs that I referred to a little while ago where you are doing this work by day's labour.
Oh, yes, this is the kind of work that can only be done advantageously by day's work.

Leave out that word
"only." That is not correct.

I shall be very glad to
have any suggestion my hon. friend may make as to how I will express it, but that is the idea: work and repair of this kind can be done much more advantageously by day's labour. I think my hon. friend agreed with me a year ago in regard to a similar repair to this, that it could be doDe better by day's labour than by contract.

That is quite correct as applied to one of the jobs, but it does not apply to the whole work. But my principal point is that I thought you would have completed this work this year.
I cannot yet see why that was mot done. The item is not very large and you are taking quite a risk in not completing the work. It might be that the $5,000 you spent on that shed' wharf that year will be wiped away simply because you have not completed the job.

I know my horn, friend
wants to be reasonable. He will bear in mind that we spent $10,000 on the other wharf last year and that we are now trying to fix up the wharf that seems to be most in need of repair. I should like to call to his attention the many wharves throughout this country which are in need of repair, and with the money we have at our disposal we are trying to look after the ones which are in greatest danger and where the work is most urgent.
I cannot say more to my hon. friend.

I hope I am not unreasonable-I realize the difficulties of the minister-but I point out to him the fact that he would not have found it necessary to spend one dollar on these wharves at all if he had allowed the Department of Railways and.

Canals to look after its own property. speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering the item "Port Maitland-breakwater extension, to complete payments, $3,500."
Mr. Chairman, we had not passed, as I understand it, the item referred to just above that, "Port Greville-groynes". I asked the minister a question, and he was answering it when the house rose.

I think I mentioned, Mr. Chairman, to my hon. friend, that this amount of $2,000 is required to construct two parallel pile and waling groynes each 300 feet long and about 400 feet apart. The proposed work is requested by the district engineer. The drift of gravel at this place is to the east and towards the breakwater. A gravel bar extends past the breakwater several hundred feet. Schooners loaded with lumber and piling have difficulty navigating the crooked entrance channel which has a very sharp turn through the bar. It is anticipated that the proposed work will form a trap and prevent the drift
from going past the breakwater. The river and tidal flow from the harbour basin could overcome the obstruction at the entrance and maintain the entrance in a stable condition. A public wharf, a number of private wharves and a shipbuilding plant are located at this place. Shipments consist of approximately five million feet of lumber annually.

Is this protection work to take place of the proposed extension to the breakwater as suggested by me some years ago? A new breakwater was constructed there considerably shorter than the old one, and the shortness of the break-wafer has caused the formation of this bar which the minister mentions. Do I understand from the minister that this is to take place of the extension to the breakwater? I would also like to ask whether any provision is 'being made .this year to repair what is commonly called the beach protection at this point. This beach protection protects the channel of the harbour so that it keeps it clear from gravel drifts and sediment and allows vessels to pass in and out. Is any provision being made to repair this protection?

I would say to my hon. friend that the breakwater 'built in 1924-26 is a protection work out at the end of the beach protection work, and curving off at an angle. The object of the proposed groynes is to stop the drift. They are located near the centre of the protection work, and it is thought that they will stop the drifting which has been occurring there.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with this item I may say that there are two wharves at this particular point. One is what is known as the government railway wharf and the other the Public Works wharf. May I point out that within the last couple of years, Mr. Cyrus S. Eaton, a well known financier who was born in the vicinity of Pugwash, and who has won considerable fame for his prowess in the financial world on the other side of the border line, generously offered to beautify the waterfront there, to which end he has spent many thousands of dollars in building a sea-wall and making other improvements. Those two wharves, which are more or less in a dilapidated condition, are almost at one end of the work being done by Mr. Eaton. There are some buildings in between, but they are in close proximity to the work that he has undertaken to beautify the town of Pugwash. It seems to me that the least the government can do is to [DOT] put those public services in such a condition that they will not be, as they are to-day, a disgrace to that portion of the water-front. Moreover, I am told by those who are in a position to know, that in recent times they have inspected the wharves and they are both in need of what they call new decks. I am also told that the ballast at the end of both the railway wharf and the Public Works wharf has rolled out into the channel and filled it up so that large steamers, when they enter, frequently go aground and considerable dredging is required to make the channel free. This is one case where a special appeal can be made and I urge the minister to give this matter serious consideration. Mr. Eaton is endeavouring to do everything possible to beautify the place and also to make it commercially advantageous to those who live there. Therefore the least the government can do is to put those services in a proper state of repair. This is an important point on the Northumberland straits and a great deal of shipping passes through there annually. Will the minister give some consideration to the observations I have made?

The hon. member has referred to the two services, and by that I understand he means the Canadian National Railways wharf and the Public Works wharf. The Canadian National Railways wharf is still under the Department of Railways and Canals and we are repairing only the portion of that wharf which is under the jurisdiction of this department. The statement made by Assistant Engineer Bennett is that the wharf

has been damaged by ice and that repairs are absolutely necessary to the lumber shipping, especially since the Canadian National Railways wharf is in a bad state of repair. This corroborates what my hon. friend has said. The bulk of the lumber has to be handled over the Public Works wharf. That is the one we are proposing to repair.
Mr, SMITH (Cumberland):	The item
reads "repairs to departmental railway wharf." Is that an error?

No; that is the departmental wharf that has the railway connection to it. The other wharf has not any railway connection to it. This is distinguishing the departmental wharf from the other so as to make it clear to which wharf these repairs shall apply. It is the departmental wharf which has the railway connection.
Will the minister take into consideration the question of repairs to both those services? That is what I am anxious to know and what the people there are concerned about.

I am afraid there is no
object in my taking into consideration repairs to a wharf that is not under the jurisdiction of this department. There is no use in my saying I will do so, because the other wharf is not under my jurisdiction.

Unfortunately that is a situation that should not exist. For the last two or three years negotiations have been carried on between the railway department and the Public Works department with respect to the Public Works taking over the railway wharf. I do not know how much longer these negotiations are going to last, but in the meantime that particular wharf is going to pieces. The railways are doing nothing about it. The Public Works department say they can do nothing about it; that it belongs to the railways. Something should be decided very soon in this matter so that this service can be put in a fit condition.
Does my hon. friend suggest that we should take over the railway wharf?

I am not suggesting anything about it, except this, that the wharf ought to be repaired by either the government or the railways, and that if the railways refuse to repair it, the government should take it over and put it into a state of repair. It does not matter under whose jurisdiction it is, it should be repaired.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, NR.

The argument made by
one of my hon. friend's colleagues in the house this afternoon was that we should not have taken over a similar wharf at Pictou. I just wonder whether my hon. friends are in agreement with regard to this policy. At any rate we have not taken over the wharf and we shall not make any repairs to it until we do. Whether or not we shall take it over in the future -is a matter for consideration. We are, however, doing our best to repair the wharf which is under our jurisdiction.

What is the length of the
wharf now and how long will it be after the extension is added?

This amount is required
for constructing an extension 40 -feet by 80 feet to the present breakwater, widening the present vessel bed by 10 feet and extending it for a distance of 50 feet. The proposed work is requested by the district engineer who reports that the work is necessary to accommodate the increasing export trade at this place. The existing wharf is 250 feet in length and steamers of 280 feet can load only two hatches at one time. The export trade there consists of shipping apples to European ports, 90,000 ban-els being shipped last season. It is anticipated that with the proposed improvements, from 150,000 to 250,000 barrels of apples will be shipped annually.

I thank the minister for
the information. I want to do what I seldom do when the minister's estimates are before the committee; I want to say a word about that wharf at Port Williams. I do not know of any other investment the governmemt has ever made that has yielded to date more tremendous dividends than the investment on that wharf. About 815,000 was voted in 1927 to take over the wharf, and during this apple shipping season alone, 95,000 -barrels of apples were shipped over tlh-e wharf to Great Britain and other European countries at an estimated saving of 40 cents per ban-el, the shippers being saved S38,000 in one season on an investment of 815,000. More than that, under the Maritime Freight Rates Act the government of Canada is obliged to pay one-fifth of the freight rate on apples going via Halifax and that is the way those apples would go if they did not go over this wharf. That would mean the government of Canada would be obliged to pay something over $6,000 to the railway company if the apples did not go over this wharf. I thought it worth while
to bring these facts to the attention of the minister and the committee. We sometimes hear it said that money invested in breakwaters or wharves in Nova Scotia is to a considerable extent wasted, but I will venture to say there are very few members of the house who have heard of an investment of the government that has yielded or could be expected to yield greater dividends to shippers or to the government than has the investment in this wharf.

Yes. I might proceed
with that and give my hon. friend the information which he desired. I find on glancing over the file during the recess that the contract for this work was let on the first of September, 1928. As it has a bearing upon the labour conditions and the attitude taken bv the government in regard thereto, I will give briefly the history. On the first of September, 1928, the contractors, Messrs. Boone and Voye, were duly advised by letter from the chief engineer .that the authority of council was being obtained to accept their tender amounting to $18,190 at the unit prices quoted, the work to be fully and satisfactorily completed on or before the first of September, 1929. He added that a formal contract would be submitted for their signature within a few days. The contractors were also advised that the contract contained a clause in connection with .the fair wage requirements. Then the order in council was passed and the contract awarded. It will be observed that under this contract the work was to be done by the first of September, 1929. On August 31 a telegram was received by the chief engineer as follows: Reference Barrington ice pier number five under contract Boone and Voye. Progress of work unsatisfactory and consider interest to public and department require department complete this work under terms of said contract. Chronologically the record is: contractors notified by you September first 1928; September 28th contractors visited site of work with assistant enginers Gregory and Allison; September 11th contractors informed me that hardwood timber could not be procured until next spring; during April 1929 I informed contractors of necessity early commencement work; on May 7th they informed me timber would not be ready until September; after considerable discussion I ordered timber to be creosoted Truro immediately; after considerable negotiations with Canada Creosoting Company, timber was creosoted early in June, first car being delivered Barrington June 22nd; this timber should have been delivered there; contractors made no efforts towards dredging pier seat until hardly pressed by me, when they entered into contract with Beacon Dredging company to perform said dredging; on July 1st work was commenced-

on construction on shore of crib for pier; on July 2nd, dredge tried to excavate material but unsuccessfully; consider dredge too small for this work and. arranged for Leconfield on way Brooklyn to perform said dredging; July thirtieth and thirty-first Leconfield attempted to dredge pier seat, found not feasible, therefore requested contractor to lay foundation of pier on present surface, evening u,p said foundation and then to place piers on same; contractor has made no progress since. I notice the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) is in his seat, and before these Nova Scotia items are disposed of I would call his attention to a matter to which I referred this afternoon. The proof of that is here in my hand, and I can give the minister the names of the twenty-six workmen.

The only reply I can make to that is that it had not 'been brought to my attention. The prevailing rate of wages in that district is not $2.50.

Necessary and urgent matters, and suggestions such as that brought forward by my hon. friend who just spoke, will receive careful consideration.

Is there anything in the
departmental estimates for Campbellton and that vicinity? I have not had time to go through the estimates, I may say frankly, and I should like to know if there is anything for dredging at Campbellton on the Restigouche river.

It probably will be done,
but I cannot say positively. We get all these recommendations and we have to do the things that seem necessary.

Of course the minister
knows that this is a very important point, and that practically all the developments in

New Brunswick in the last few years have been on the Restigouche river. I know the companies with which I am connected are very heavy importers and shippers from that point; practically all that shipping is done on the New Brunswick side. The minister's colleague

While we are appreciative of what has been done in regard to estimates for tlm maritime provinces, there are some items which have been overlooked. Within the past year I attended a meeting of the board of trade of the town of Shediac at which the Postmaster General was present, and we visited a place in the county of Westmorland known as Point du Chene, where there is a small wharf. At present that wharf is in a very dilapidated condition and is unsafe for traffic; it really is a disgrace to the department and to the government of the day. At that time the Postmaster General stated that he would see to it that these wharves would be fixed up and put in shape. I believe he intended to carry out his statement, at any rate at the time he made it. In previous years thousands of dollars worth of sea food such as lobster, oysters, clams and so on passed over this wharf, and I believe the Postmaster General had every intention of seeing that this wharf was put in order. However,
I note that in these estimates not one cent has been allowed for that work. Of course I do not know whether or not it is the intention to bring down something in the supplementary estimates to look after these repairs; perhaps that will be done, but at any rate the wharf

at Point du Chene has been overlooked, together with the Shediac wharf, and I want to say to the Minister of Public Works and to the Postmaster General that the people in my constituency will hold the government of the day accountable for their neglect in this regard.
I should also like to dfaw attention to the fact that within the last year the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was notified of the fact that one of the mooring posts on the public wharf at Moncton had decayed to such a point that it broke off while a ship was moored there with a cargo of lumber, and the result was that two individuals from Pre d'en haut in my constituency were drowned. Morally the Department of Public Works is responsible for those deaths, although legally that may not be the case. I have appealed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, asking that some allowance be made the dependents of these men; the parents of one of the men are over seventy years of age and I have asked that something be done for them by way of a compassionate allowance, but no action has been taken. I believe there is some possibility of such an allowance being made during this session, and I do hope the minister will see his way clear to recommending it.
I must add that in my constituency the Department of Public Works has entirely failed to maintain properly the wharves and other public undertakings. I believe the Postmaster General will bear me out when I say that the wharves in particular have been absolutely neglected and allowed to rot to such an extent that they are not safe for the use of the general public.
There is one further matter which I should like to bring up, and that is in regard to the construction of a post office in the city of Moncton, which turns into the revenue of this country about $388,000 per year, or an average of over SI,000 per day. On several occasions the attention of the government has been called to the fact that the post office building in that city is in a miserable and dilapidated condition; it is a menace to the public, unsanitary and unsuitable in every way for the use of the public and those who are handling the mails and endeavouring to give the public proper service.

It was not my intention to take any part in the debate on these estimates, but since the hon. member who represents the county of Westmorland has thought fit to say that he was sure I would agree with him when he said that the Department of Public Works had neglected the wharves and other structures in the county of Westmorland,

Supply-Harbours and Rivers, N.B.
I rise to say that I cannot agree with a statement which in my opinion is not founded on
fact.
The hon. member has referred to the wharf at Point du Chene. If he had wanted to tell the whole truth he would have told the house that the wharf does not belong to the Department of Public Works at all, but it is controlled by the Department of Railways and Canals. The facts are that when the Cape Tormentine route w'as opened this wharf was practically abandoned, and from that time on the Canadian National Railways never paid very much attention to it and let it go to destruction. It is true that now it is in a scandalous condition and unsafe, but the blame should be placed not on the government or on the Department of Public Works, but on the Canadian National Railways. It is true I visited Point du Chene in company with the hon. gentleman representing the county of Westmorland (Mr. Price) and members of the board of trade and city council, and I there and then said that I would make as strong representations as I possibly could to the Department of Public Works or to the railway for either the railway to repair the wharf or the Department of Public Works to take it over. It will cost about 8130,000 to put this wharf in repair- not the whole of it, but sufficient of it to meet the traffic conditions as they exist at the present time. The Canadian National Railways draw a revenue of from 828.000 to 830,000 a year from the traffic that is landed at that wharf, placed aboard the cars and shipped to the United States and sections of Canada. The Canadian National Railways have refused to contribute anything to the upkeep or repair of this wharf, and they want the Public Works department to take it over at an expenditure of 8130,000 to 8140,000. I have been trying to convince the Canadian National Railways that since they are getting a revenue out of it it is up to them to keep this wharf in repair. So far I have not succeeded in convincing Sir Henry Thornton that I am right and he is wrong. I am not the first one who has been' unable to convince him of a thing of that kind, and it is not surprising that I have not succeeded up to the present time. I understand negotiations are proceeding between the Department of Public Works and the railway authorities at Montreal touching this very wharf. Those are the facts. If my hon. friend had told those facts as I relate them now it would have been better instead of trying to put the blame upon the Department of Public Works. I know something about the hon. gentleman's
county and no doubt he is aware that I do. Last year I visited every wharf and every harbour in the province of New Brunswick excepting one county which I could not reach, and I know the condition of nearly every harbour and wharf in that province with the exception of that one county. My hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) was very fair this afternoon in referring to certain wharves that have been repaired. After this year there will not be a wharf owned by the Department of Public Works on the whole St. John river that will not be in first class repair, not only repaired in wood but reconstructed in concrete. Those wharves were taken over in 1920-21 from the government of New Brunswick. I had the honour of being provincial Minister of Public Works at that time, and those wharves were found to be in a very dilapidated condition owing to the fact that the provincial government could not afford to repair them. Last summer, as I visited every wharf on the St. John river- the wharf referred to by the hon. member for York-Sunbury as well-I found, with the exception recommended by me to the Department of Public Works, every wharf on the river St. John as well as on the Ken-nebecasis river and the Belleisle, in first class condition. I visited the wharves in the county of Westmorland, and I also visited the most important section of wharf construction in Westmorland county. There excellent work is being done, and it is not fair for the hon. member for the county of Westmorland to state that the Department of Public Works has absolutely neglected the wharves in that county.

They certainly have been
neglected.

The hon. gentleman knows
that I am telling the truth.
I know that you are not.

Take that back. I doubt
very much whether the hon. gentleman has visited many of those wharves, and there are not many wharves in the county of Westmorland owned by the Department of Public Works. The greater number of the wharves on the Petitcodiac river, and the most important, are owned by private owners, and if these wharves are in a dilapidated condition-
What about Cape Bald?
I referred to that.

Just explain Cape Bald. Put yourself on record.

The wharf at Cape Bald
is a construction which was started about twenty years ago, built absolutely of concrete, one of the best constructed wharves there is in the whole maritime provinces. True, it was destroyed or put out of repair in certain sections owing to the very severe storms along that coast, but the necessary repairs have been made. With the development that has taken place they have to-day at Cape Bald a breakwater that protects the harbour, and it is one of the best and most substantial wharves in the whole maritime provinces. I know something about construction; I have had ten or twelve years' experience in the matter.
Mr. PRICE Why enlarge the wharf now?

Because the time has arrived when the wharf in its present condition does not meet the requirements of the fishermen and the department are giving them the requirements to meet the case so that they will have better protection than they have been getting in the past few years.

How many boats have been
destroyed in the last few years on those shores as a result of the neglect of the present administration? Why is the government only now bringing down an estimate for $10,000 for repairs?	-

I will do what an Irish friend of mine does-answer my hon, friend's question by asking him another one. How many boats and schooners and even lives were lost during the time my hon. friends were in power on account of their neglect in the matter of looking after the Cape Bald breakwater? They did not spend a dollar on it from 1912 to 1918 or 1919.
I suppose the Postmaster General remembers that there was a war on then.

There was no war on between 1911 and 1914 or between 1919 and 1921. My hon. friends had five or six years in which to make the repairs.
Let me come to the statement made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury. It is true the city of Fredericton has a wharf, not wharves. It has what is known as a combined high and low tide wharf. The city of Frederioton the year before last spent on the maintainance of that wharf between $8,000 and 810,000. I visited that wharf last September, I think it was, accompanied by the mayor and members of the city council. I went over the wharf carefully. The federal engineer, under instructions from the Depart-

ment of Public Works, accompanied me. I have recommended to the Department of Public Works the taking over of that wharf from the city of Fredericton, and the matter is now under consideration. But let me point this out: there is a government wharf within the limits of the city of Fredericton, but it is above the bridge; it is a concrete wharf and it has been used in the pa9t only for tugboats handling rafts or something of that kind, shallow boats drawing very little water. But the wharf at Fredericton owned by the city is a very important one, and I have hopes that when all the negotiations have been concluded, the Department of Public Works may see its way clear to look with favour upon the taking over of that wharf. The city council of Fredericton had not previously intimated to the Department of Public Works that they had passed a resolution authorizing the turning over of the wharf to the government. Yesterday I received from the mavor of Fredericton a letter in which he informed me that the city council, only the night before, had passed such a resolution, authorizing certain officials to get into communication with the Department of Public Works with the view of offei'ing the wharf to the government. They are not asking any price for it; they are giving it gratis; they feel that they themselves cannot afford to maintain it. The estimate for repairs to put the wharf into proper condition is $110,000. It is impossible to leave it in its present condition. Some repairs must be made to it and negotiations are now pending, so I am informed, between the city authorities and the Department of Public Works.

I have no complaint to make about the statement of the Postmaster General with respect to the Fredericton wharf. All I would like to announce is that if the wharf is not taken over by the present government, we will take it over after the next election.
That will be ten years from now.

Item agreed to.
Shippigan Gully-repairs to breakwaters and breastworks, $15,000.

This is rather an important item. How much money has been spent at Shippigan Gully in the last ten years? I cannot remember a session when there has not been a large sum of money voted for Shippigan Gully. What is the necessity for it? Is it the yearly annual allowance for the people in that community to live on, or what is it? It does seem to me that there ought to be some let-<up in the expenditure of public money at that point. Like some individuals who are never off the payroll of the country, Shippigan Gully never seems to be out of the estimates.

I understand that these
works were started away back in 1875, which would be long before my hon. friend was born, and they have been carried on with reasonable diligence from time to time since. This

There seems to be an impression in the mind of the hon. member for York-Sunbury that this is a sort of yearly grant to the people of Shippigan. To my mind that is a reflection upon the hardy fishermen and upon the honest folk of the mainland of Shippigan.
If the hon. gentleman knew the history of this undertaking, I am sure that he would recognize at once the necessity of keeping it up. It is true that Shippigan Gully breakwater was started as far back as 1875, but at that time there was no intention to make it the very important structure that it is to-day. It was not really started at all at that time. Shippigan Gully, up to fifteen or twenty years ago, had only four feet of water at low tide at the entrance to the gully. As the fishing fleets of Caraquet, Lower Caraquet, Little Lameque and St. Simon increased, these works had to be added to. The Department of Public Works at that time, instead of dredging yearly to try to keep this channel open, undertook to construct a breakwater of immense proportions, which was necessary, and directed the flow of tide in and out to such an extent that after dredging the gully to a depth of 14 feet, that depth was able to be maintained by the current itself. To-day no less than 350 fishing sail, ranging all the way from twenty to fifty tons, use weekly this entrance to Shippigan harbour. In former years, instead of being able to go through Shippigan Gully, they had to make the round of East Point Miscou, a distance of forty-one miles, but by the construction of these works these vessels can come in a direct run of about four hours from the shipping banks of Prince Edward Island, thus saving a run of over fifty miles by having to go round East Point Miscou. Anyone who would attempt to belittle the department for making an expenditure of this kind certainly does not know what he is talking about.

I am very much obliged
to the Postmaster General for his scolding, though it really does not matter a bit what he thinks of me. I was simply pointing out that the public are entitled to know why year after year there is this very large expenditure
(Mr. Elliott.)
at Shippigan. I quite realize that over half the estimates for New Brunswick are in the county of my hon. friend, but that does not help the rest of the province very much.
